No one stole jazz from anyone, but it wasn't "invented" out of thin air. A good portion of it comes from the teachings of the impressionists in France, who were using compositional techniques that were virtually unknown in the music schools (at least within America). French impressionist music was extremely popular in French-speaking parts of America (where there were many black people). Furthermore, the academies stagnated as they used traditional methods of analysis, which struggled with polytonality and pan/non-diatonic harmony. Jazz is much, much simpler than the academies made it seem, as they were over-analyzing it with the wrong tools.

Some of the differences with early jazz music that the academies got wrong (at some point) include:

  • Complex melodies usually came from enclosure/embellishment of chord tones, rather than pure scales (although scales were used)
  • Harmony was organized diatonically, but each diatonic chord was connected by inversions of diminished chords (see diminished six scale)
  • Diatonic chords could borrow notes from surrounding diminished chords, and visa versa (no over-analyzing complex chords)
  • Any triad when stacked on top of a dominant, functions as a dominant.
  • You can modulate between chord qualities so long as there are common tones
  • Diminished chords are connected to 4 separate dominant chords, and hence 4 separate keys, via common tones. Each of those chords dominant chords can function as substitutes.
  • Each chord can be lead either chromatically, or with secondary non-diatonic chords.
  • Harmonies (like the ii V I) can modulate through various keys, but modulations are smoother if there are more common tones between keys. Giant steps, considered one of the more complex jazz pieces, is literally ii V I's modulating through keys separated by major 3rds (basically an augmented triad).

Few jazz musicians understood music theory, they didn't have to. Instead, they had a much simpler visceral understanding of music. Jazz was, in essence, the next evolution of classical music. But it was also a hodgepodge combination of many, many styles. Dixieland jazz was heavily influenced by ragtime and Sicilian music. The defining element of ragtime was its syncopated rhythms, that came out of romantic-era march music (see John Philip Sousa), in combination with African rhythm. Dixieland jazz and ragtime were both influences in gypsy jazz, which was key in popularizing certain harmony, rhythms and embellished arpeggios.

I could go on, but the point is that jazz didn't come from one place, and it certainly wasn't invented out of thin air by black people. Most of the teachings came from the impressionists, combined with various ethnic styles.
